rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.3-2.4 and 3 <U+2014> the authors run their own GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation (AHP weighted overlay of seven factors) for Uganda and report their own suitability maps and area statistics for baseline and two climate scenarios.
rows.notes: The study is a GIS/AHP land-suitability mapping exercise for surface irrigation under current and projected climate in Uganda. It does not involve artificial intelligence, machine learning from historical data, app-based irrigation scheduling, or any measurement of irrigation management performance, efficiency or water conservation. Its result is the spatial extent of land in each suitability class (e.g., 0.9% highly suitable, 32.4% moderately suitable) and how these shift under warming scenarios. The AHP weights are expert-judgement based, not learned from data. Ground truthing is limited to noting that existing schemes fall in moderately suitable areas. Hence no own evidence on the claimed technology or effect; the technology (GIS-MCE land suitability) differs from the one in the passage (AI-based scheduling decision support).

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a national-scale GIS land suitability assessment, cited by the review for a claim about AI-driven irrigation decision-making; the mismatch is between a planning-level suitability map and an operational scheduling tool.
